c4f1da693af6b0106ffedb87215e9996f229b02b.summary: CrowdStrike blog on removable-media risk, covering data theft by insiders and malicious devices entering endpoints. Its main case study is MUSTANG PANDA's USBFect USB worm campaigns (2023 to 2025), which used loaders to deliver LingerRAT, spread from the Philippines to Taiwan, and were later seen affecting organisations in North America. It also cites late 2025 USB-delivered CoinMiner campaigns and a 2025 case in which a U.S. defense engineer admitted moving over 3,600 files to personal storage. The text promotes CrowdStrike Falcon Data Protection and Falcon Device Control.

c44102b7092e8536bff0af1b062bbf436d3f3966.summary: Joint research by Flashpoint and RiskIQ, relayed by KrebsOnSecurity in November 2018, describes hundreds of fake e-commerce shops set up on expired domains to skim payment card data. The report counts more than 800 such sites since June 2018 and links them to Magecart, described as a collective of at least seven cybercrime groups. Stolen card data is sold in online cybercrime shops, and some actors sell live access to hacked stores. Two non-commercial anti-abuse organisations and Shadowserver help sinkhole hacked domains.

c4fb1d1834fd0a9e2e38a8b863841bd820c757b3.summary: Joint US government advisory (CISA, Treasury, FBI, USCYBERCOM) on the group it calls BeagleBoyz, described as part of North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, which robs banks through remote access. Covers the FASTCash ATM cash-out malware for AIX and Windows payment switch servers, fraudulent SWIFT terminal activity, and cryptocurrency exchange heists. Names tools including CROWDEDFLOUNDER, HOPLIGHT, ELECTRICFISH and COPPERHEDGE, lists techniques and targeted countries, and gives an estimate of nearly $2 billion stolen since 2015. Includes mitigation advice for financial institutions.

hedges: The technical analysis represents an amalgamation of multiple known incidents, rather than details of a single operation.
The BeagleBoyz overlap to varying degrees with groups tracked by the cybersecurity industry as Lazarus, APT38, Bluenoroff and Stardust Chollima.

The BeagleBoyz may also be working with or contracting out to criminal hacking groups, such as TA505.
The BeagleBoyz appear to have modified publicly available source code, and likely change tools over time.
The nearly $2 billion figure is based on public estimates.
The group is likely active since at least 2014 and is likely a major source of funding for North Korea.
